sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿**COMMENTS**
This Composite Source straddles the marine region from Mt. Conero (to the northwest) toward the Mid-Adriatic Deep (to the southeast), stemming SE-ward from the Umbro-Marche Apennines outer onshore thrust front. This front is the NE-verging outermost fault system of the Northern Apennines chain, well into the central Adriatic Sea.
Historical and instrumental catalogues (Boschi et al., 2000; Gruppo di Lavoro CPTI, 2004; Pondrelli et al., 2006; Guidoboni et al., 2007, CPTI15) show only a sparse intermediate (4.5 < Mw < 5.0) seismicity surrounding the area, besides the 4 September 1987 (Mw 5.1, Porto San Giorgio) event that has occurred just north-west of the area.
A series of well-developed asymmetric anticlines reverse faults rooted on this main thrust, are arranged in a right-stepping, en-echelon system toward the southeast. Stratigraphic information and the fine-scale seismic data in Ridente and Trincardi (2006) confirm the structural arrangement at the southeastern sector of this system and its current activity, thanks to the spatial and chronological data resolution. Size and geometry of the active thrust splays suggest a plausible seismogenic potential. It is interesting to notice that this source is very close to the westernmost front of the Dinarides thrusts in the central Adriatic Sea. As a matter of fact Scrocca (2006) highlights the juxtaposition of the two sources, and maintains that the structure just to the east of the Western Mid-Adriatic offshore Source dips to the W-SW and thus belongs to the Apennines outer thrust system. However, the geometry of the eastern anticline interpreted by Scrocca (2006) does not show a clear asymmetry like the western structure does. This could be due to the extents of the available seismic line to the east, but it does leave room for an opposite interpretation - i.e. that the western fault-propagation anticline belongs to the outer Apennine system, while the facing one has an eastern dip and belong to the outer Dinarides.
